EICMA 2026 • 2027 Suzuki SV-7S Unveiled at the EICMA Show in Italy: I’m Suddenly More Nostalgic Than Ever
Volvo Announces Refreshed XC40, EX40, EC40 Pricing for the UK, Also the XC90 T8 Long Range PHEV
50 photos
Photo: Volvo
Volvo Car UK aims to conquer the local market with the mid-cycle refresh of the compact XC40, EX40, EC40 crossover SUVs and also a flagship CUV – the long-range version of the XC90 T8 plug-in hybrid.
The Swedish automaker may not feel all too well globally with dwindling profits during the third quarter of the year, but over in the United Kingdom the local division Volvo Car UK won’t be issuing any complaints: during the third quarter of this year, Volvo registered 18,991 cars in the UK, up nearly six percent compared to last year and also nailed a September record in the process.
As such, it’s no wonder the company aims to keep up the good times by announcing the latest novelties for customers: Volvo Car UK has launched the refreshed 40 series range, which is now available for order in the country. Three models are available: the mild-hybrid XC40 , as well as the fully electric EX40 and EC40 coupe-SUV.
All three of them “feature significant design, technology and safety enhancements,” and on-the-road pricing kicks off at £37,710 (around $50k at the current exchange rate) for the XC40, from £43,860 (over $58k) for the EX40 and £45,860 (over $61k) for the EC40. The facelift brings “a more confident interpretation of Volvo’s Scandinavian design language.”
So, all three of them have redesigned front bumpers, hoods, and front wings, an upgraded grille, and new Thor’s Hammer Matrix LED headlights with 15-segment adaptive lighting technology. Around the back, the XC40 and EX40 have new LED rear lights, a revised tailgate, and a redesigned bumper, while the EC40 doesn’t have changes. The XC40 also has new diamond-cut wheels in 18-, 19- and 20-inch sizes.
Moving inside, the three refreshed siblings have a larger 11.2-inch center touchscreen with Volvo’s latest user interface, an improved wireless phone charger, premium upholstery and décor options, smart storage and “refined” cabin illumination. XC40 customers can also add Arianne Cardamom leather upholstery with Brown Ash wood.
The Volvo XC40 comes to the UK with the B3 and B4 gasoline mild-hybrid engines and a seven-speed automatic, while the EX40 has the P5 Long Range Plus specification with RWD or AWD and a range of up to 354 miles. The EC40 has the same trim for RWD but switches to P8 for AWD, and the range is up to 359 miles on a charge.
Additionally, Volvo also said it has opened the order books for the XC90 T8 Long Range plug-in hybrid flagship crossover SUV. It comes with the latest design update, “with styling that reflects Scandinavian luxury,” and the popular big CUV additionally welcomes a new long-range hybrid powertrain with up to 101 miles of electric range, which is more than double its predecessor’s performance.
UK on-the-road prices start at £66,270 (over $88k) for the B5 mild hybrid version, and the new T8 Long Range plug-in hybrid starts at £75,765 or about $101k! The T8 Long Range plug-in hybrid has a combined 461 horsepower and can sprint to 62 mph in just 5.2 seconds. Inside, there’s room for seven, an 11.2-inch center touchscreen with Volvo's latest user interface, quilted Nordico and ventilated Nappa soft leather, as well as Google Gemini, Google's conversational AI assistant, which is also offered on the refreshed 40 series.
Safety remains paramount for Volvo, with the XC90 and 40 series, with the latter gaining an updated sensor and software platform with new radar and camera technology and 12 ultrasonic sensors. The flagship SUV has Pilot Assist, adaptive cruise control, Blind Spot Information System with Steer Assist, and City Safety with automatic braking, plus Automatic Matrix LED headlights with adaptive shadow technology, among others.

Policy uncertainty is hampering the growth of U.S. biotech as China rises thanks to carefully planned investment in the industry, experts said during a BioSpace webinar.
Strand Therapeutics CEO Jake Becraft grew up in the Rust Belt. He knows what the end of a massive industry can look like. Now, he’s watching Chinese biotechs threaten to overtake America’s homegrown life sciences industry.
“If you come down the Illinois River, you can see the beach littered with the skeletons of a once producing nation that now no longer produces almost anything in our critical supply chain outside of defense products,” Becraft said during a BioSpace webinar last month . Living in Boston, he already sees the parallels to his Midwest home.
“The saddest thing in the world would be for Kendall Square to look like where I grew up, just a bunch of empty warehouses littered,” Becraft said. “But to be honest, a lot of that lab space is empty right now.”
China
6 potential blockbusters that could pave China’s path to 2030 ambitions
In its latest five-year plan, China has set its sights on developing five drugs that could each rake in more than $1 billion globally by 2030. Experts say it’s well on its way, with two medications having already met that bar.
November 4, 2026
·
8 min read
·
Tristan Manalac
Read more
While lab oversupply is part of the equation in Boston, Becraft said the impact of declining investment in U.S. biotech will only grow more apparent.
U.S. biotechs are experiencing a one-two punch. China’s industry is rising, churning out investigational therapeutics that can rival or even best some of the innovation happening stateside. Big Pharma is flocking to the country to sign lucrative licensing deals . At the same time, companies are facing a devastating era of policy unpredictability, with both China and the U.S. recently proposing new restrictions on American investments in Chinese biotechs and the ownership of some intellectual property .
“That lack of predictability just really makes it hard to run a business. It actually makes it hard to run a chicken stand, let alone a biotech company,” Patrowski Lawson, founder of the consulting firm KPM Group and the American Biotech Innovation Alliance (ABIA), said on the webinar.
Lila Hope, a partner at Sidley who negotiates strategic transactions in the life sciences sector, added that these already complex deals have become more fraught as new policies are thrown around.
“This isn’t a bill of sale or something that we do today and it takes effect tomorrow and then we’re good,” Hope explained. “This is drug development. This has a long-term implication in terms of co-development, data sharing, long-term investment.”
She continued, “Out of all of this, the difficult part is we don’t know what restriction or what prohibition is going to pop up on Capitol Hill.” Even rumors of potential policies have been dogging deal negotiators like Hope.
In fact, European pharmas have been so bold as to use their position as a less complex policy environment to win multi-bid processes with Chinese pharmas, Hope said. “The negotiation power of the European pharmas and Japanese pharmas are just going to increase by comparison to the U.S. companies.”
And should China succeed in its latest five-year plan to produce more of the world’s medicines, Americans could be subject to the whim of an adversarial nation that has been deemed a threat, Becraft stressed. “The idea that the American patient would need to basically ask China’s permission for any critical medicine is completely a non-starter from a national security perspective and sovereign independence.”
China
China’s licensing deals soar as US biotechs enjoy a bumper M&A year
China may be taking the majority of licensing deals this year but those transactions don’t tell the whole story, according to Locust Walk, which points to the spike in M&A among U.S. biotechs as leveling the playing field.
October 21, 2026
·
3 min read
·
Annalee Armstrong
Read more
The U.S. has a long way to go to shift the trajectories in its favor, the panelists agreed. Lawson was blunt: “A lot of this environment is somewhat pessimistic right now because China is kicking us in the teeth. I want to be optimistic here. And think that the way forward is for us is to get our shit together.”
Spinning the flywheel
Leaders like Lawson and Jeremy Levin, co-founder and executive chair of Ovid Therapeutics, have been calling for a formalized plan to advance and protect the U.S. biotech industry. On Tuesday, BIO introduced one , with a recommendation to create a White House Office of Biotechnology, streamline clinical trials and bolster manufacturing.
The effort to grow U.S. biotech must extend beyond the industry, Levin argued. He has gone out beyond Kendall Square to talk to everyday Americans about the biotech industry to plead the case that we must support our homegrown talent and technology.
“There is a fundamental gap in the understanding of the American populace as to what we do and why people should trust us,” Levin said on the webinar. “If we don’t deal with it, we will continue to get legislation that will be harmful to us.”
None of the panelists were supportive of an outright ban on Chinese innovation.
“The best products are the best product, and that’s geographic agnostic,” Hope said. If a Big Pharma finds an asset in China, they are still bringing some piece of its value back to the U.S. and delivering the medicine to American patients.
Instead of a ban, the biotech leaders offered changes that could be made at the FDA to ease clinical trial starts—one of seven main items on BIO’s plan and the focus of recent agency initiatives—and put the agency back on track to focus on regulatory matters.
Becraft, who testified before Congress on the issue of China earlier this year, also urged that the U.S. do more to encourage clinical trial participation. He said that just 8% of the American population is ever asked to participate in a trial. Meanwhile, Australia is running four times the clinical trials that the U.S. does with one-tenth of the population.
China
China’s surging biotech sector represents both competition and lifeline for the US
As Chinese companies push beyond “me-too” drugs and the country lays out a new five-year plan targeting a $522 billion–strong biotech industry by 2030, experts say more predictable funding and regulation could help the U.S. maintain its edge.
September 23, 2026
·
8 min read
·
Shawna Williams
Read more
“My fundamental belief is that the early stage is such a critical point for innovation because it spins the flywheel,” Becraft said. Conducting this research at home in the U.S. lowers the cost of capital and provides an early entry for investors. “It opens up the capital pools that can back early-stage innovation when it’s $5 million to an answer, not $50 million to an answer.”
To help, Becraft suggested: “We actually just need the FDA to do a little bit less” and be more like Australia.
Levin agreed, explaining that, after spending plenty of time Down Under, he has seen the “extraordinary clinical trial capability” there, where hospitals have Phase 1 research embedded at their core and patients readily offered investigational options.
Both Levin and Becraft suggested that academic centers and hospitals need to get out of the way too, with institutional review boards causing unnecessary delays to test new drugs in patients.
“Frankly, what the administration could do now is crack down on that immediately,” Levin said.
Through it all, the FDA needs to maintain its true regulatory strength, the panelists agreed. Both Becraft and Levin were encouraged by the approach the latest leadership is taking after a year of tumult, but there is still a lot of work to be done to restore the agency’s regulatory power.
“If we don’t do that, no matter what we say, no matter what we do, innovation will not stop. It will simply migrate. It will go to China. Capital will follow it. Large companies will follow it,” Levin said. “And we’ll have that river with all these wrecked cars and wrecked factories on the side. And one day we’ll turn around and say, you know what? Boston was really amazing.”

EICMA 2026 • Yamaha Previews the Future of the Tenere Adventure Bikes With Mysterious 4 Concept
Honda’s All-New Avancier SUV Rendered, Is This What It Will Look Like?
6 photos
Photo: Kolesa
Do you remember the Honda Avancier ? Well, you probably do, because the original one was offered strictly as a station wagon, building on the era’s Accord and Odyssey, and it was a Japan-only model.
Production spanned between 1999 and 2003, taking place at the Sayama factory in Saitama, Japan, and this model was offered with a couple of powertrain options. The base one came with a straight-six that had a 2.3-liter displacement, and the superior one had a 3.0-liter V6. A four- and a five-speed automatic transmission, respectively, channeled the power to the wheels.
There was a 13-year hiatus between the original Honda Avancier and its successor, because the latter came out in 2016. And as you probably know, it is still around today. The model is also known as the Honda UR-V (Dongfeng Honda), and this one comes to life at Wuhan, in China, whereas the regular Avancier (GAC Honda) is made at Guangzhou.
This model is based on the Global Light Truck Platform 2, sharing its nuts and bolts with the third-generation Acura MDX. It has two gasoline engine options, which are mated either to a CVT (continuously variable transmission) or a nine-speed gearbox from ZF, depending on the configuration, and while the entry-level is front-wheel drive, the superior grade comes with all-wheel drive.
Honda’s current Avancier marketed in the People’s Republic is 189.6 inches (4,816 mm) long, 76.5 inches (1,942 mm) wide, and 65.7 inches (1,669 mm) tall. It has a 111-inch (2,820 mm) long wheelbase, and tips the scales at between under 3,800 and over 4,100 pounds (1.7-1.8+ metric tons). The Avancier was updated in 2020, getting modified front and rear fascias, and a few other things, and another mid-cycle refresh was performed three years later.
Photo: Kolesa Now, that same nameplate will be used for an entirely new high-rider. The upcoming Honda Avancier was recently teased, and it was the company’s Australian branch that dropped the official previews online. The short video has partially revealed the model from a few angles, and those teasers were used by Kolesa’ Nikita Chuyko to offer an unofficial yet quite realistic glimpse into the model that is right around the corner.
Care to discuss some of the design details? Well, up front, it features a closed-off grille, flanked by a pair of slim headlights that somewhat remind us of other models from different brands, such as the Range Rover Evoque. And they’re not the only things reminding us of the Evoque , because so do some of the hood’s styling cues.
On the sides, it features flush door handles, and the roofline is a bit arched toward the rear, ending with a pair of rather thick pillars, and a spoiler. There are more things at the rear that remind us of certain Range Rovers, like the lighting units, which mix a pair of vertical taillights with a thin light strip linking them together in the middle of the tailgate.
The Honda logo sits right below the light strip and above the Avancier emblem. The tailgate features a recess for the license plate, and seems to have a large opening. The rear bumper is quite short, and we can see a discreet diffuser attached to it.
This new design is expected to be seen on other vehicles from the Japanese company in the future, and here, we could mention the next generation Civic and the Accord, albeit with the necessary adjustments, and perhaps other modifications to easily tell these models apart.
Photo: Kolesa Word on the street is that the new-gen Honda Avancier will feature a three-row layout with seating for up to seven. Therefore, it should be more practical compared to the CR-V , and it should also be slightly larger. The cockpit will eventually open up to the camera, and we will be able to drop more lines about it when it does.
A new generation of the Honda self-charging hybrid assembly could power the next-gen Avancier, and some outlets believe that it could be based on a 2-liter four-cylinder engine, which should be updated, and details such as the output and thrust will be released in due course.
The second-gen Honda Avancier is expected to come to life in Prachinburi, Thailand, and from there, it will be exported to other countries. Australia will be on the list, and it looks like the model will also be sold in Japan, as well as perhaps other markets in the region.
It is yet unknown when the official unveiling of the new Honda Avancier will take place, but the model could be a few months away from revealing all of its secrets. When it will finally arrive at dealers, it will take on the likes of the Toyota Highlander, Kia Sorento, Mazda CX-80, and others. And before that happens, what’s your take on the design as previewed by the quoted outlet ? Do you fancy the looks?

source_document.body:
Unplugged Performance, the biggest name in Tesla aftermarket tuning, wants to keep the Cybertruck alive. The company publicly offered on Tuesday to take the Cybertruck line off Tesla’s hands, funded by a consortium of investors.
It comes just four days after Elon Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas around mid-2027, with the truck selling at roughly 12% of the 250,000 units a year Tesla planned for.
The offer
UP posted the pitch on X as “an open offer to Tesla.” The company says it fully supports putting Cybercab first and would run Cybertruck production “at no cost to Tesla’s floor space, headcount, or focus.”
In exchange, Tesla would collect a license fee plus FSD and Robotaxi network revenue on every vehicle built. UP even offered to let Cybercab get first call on battery cells. “We’ll wait our turn,” the company wrote.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
UP founder Ben Schaffer made it clear that he supports Tesla’s all-in move to autonomy, but he wants to keep the Cybertruck program alive.
And it isn’t stopping at the pickup. UP says it would build the Cybertruck, a three-row “CyberSUV,” and an unmanned “CyberCargo” hauler. Two vehicles Tesla has sometimes referenced, but they were never unveiled.
The post passed 240,000 views within hours, and the replies are mostly Cybertruck owners and Tesla shareholders begging Musk to say yes. Neither Musk nor Tesla had publicly responded at the time of writing.
UP has a lot riding on this. It sells an entire Cybertruck product line, the UP Invincible lift and armor kits, and it has scored several contracts to turn Cybertrucks into police vehicles for law enforcement agencies. CEO Ben Schaffer once described the company’s purpose as doing “the things that Tesla maybe wants to do, but doesn’t have the bandwidth to do.” This is that idea taken to its extreme.
Musk’s reason vs. the real one
Musk framed the Cybertruck’s end as a space problem. He said Tesla needs to “make room for increased Cybercab production.”
If the Cybertruck program was successful, Tesla wouldn’t be killing it. Tesla also produces Model Ys at Giga Texas, and it is not shutting that down to make room for Cybercab.
As we reported when Tesla announced the wind-down , that explanation doesn’t hold up. Giga Texas has more than 10 million square feet of floor space, the Cybertruck line runs at about a quarter of its 125,000-unit installed capacity, and Texas had only a few hundred Cybercabs registered as of late October.
The real problem is buyers. Tesla delivered 8,295 “Other Models” in Q3, and we estimated 7,000 to 8,000 of those were Cybertrucks , a pace of about 30,000 trucks a year. That was a good quarter by Cybertruck standards.
Even that number flatters it. S&P Global Mobility data showed SpaceX bought 1,279 Cybertrucks in Q4 2025 , about 18% of US registrations that quarter. Tesla also tried a cheaper RWD trim, killed it, launched a $60,000 AWD version, then raised prices by $5,000 in August . None of it fixed demand.
Electrek’s Take
I’ll give UP credit for this: the offer calls Musk’s bluff. If the Cybertruck is really dying because Cybercab needs the room, here’s someone volunteering to take the line off Tesla’s plate. Problem solved.
Of course, it’s more complicated than that.
There are many ways this could fail or never happen in the first place, but there’s also a slight possibility that makes this possible.
First off, the backlash is real. If you look on social media and forums, yes, most of the discussion is about how Cybertruck is a failure, and Elon is lying about why Tesla is killing it, but there’s also a serious group of people, especially Cybertruck owners, who are genuinely upset that Tesla is killing the program because they love their trucks.
Most people have never driven a Cybertruck, but the steer-by-wire makes it a very addictive vehicle to drive, and even though the price is high, the value proposition for the specs is not bad compared to the very limited options for electric pickup trucks.
In other words, I wouldn’t necessarily bet against this effort, especially if they add an SUV variant and show the program some love with some tweaks here and there.
I could see a group of wealthy Cybertruck fans pooling money under Unplugged to make this happen, but getting Tesla to agree could be hard. It’s not unheard of for an automaker to sell a vehicle program to a dealer, like the Lotus Seven and Studebaker Avanti, but it would be a first at this scale.

You could make sense of it by looking at UP to Tesla as AMG to Mercedes. It’s not too big a stretch, considering UP isn’t just your average Tesla tuner. It even worked with the automaker on its own version of the Model S Plaid .
If UP were to become for Tesla what AMG has become for Mercedes, it could make some sense for the company to run a separate vehicle program that started under Tesla, but even as I write this, I realize that there’s very little chance this will happen.
But I wish them the best of luck, and I would be happy to see the Cybertruck live on.

EICMA 2026 • Benelli Showed the World Its New Tornado Naked Tre 903 Concept at EICMA 2026 and It's a Triple!
Acura Urban Spec Trim Is a Fresh Limited Edition for 2027 Integra, ADX, and MDX Focused on Style
7 photos
Photo: Acura
The premium Japanese brand of American Honda has created the curated Acura Urban Spec grade for the 2027 model year of the Integra compact liftback, ADX subcompact luxury crossover SUV, and the popular MDX mid-size CUV.
American Honda recently pledged no less than $3 billion in investments in the United States focused on hybrids via multiple facilities, including a new auto plant in Central Ohio, as it said that it wants to “meet growing customer demand for hybrid vehicles in North America.” Both the namesake Honda brand and the premium Acura division will benefit from the additional investments as the company seeks to increase local production to about 1.3 million units annually and no less than 1.9 million in total across North America.
Well, Acura needs all the help it can get because although American Honda announced the best October month across the US automotive market in six years, the 8% growth to 120k units was entirely supported by the namesake Honda brand (+9.1%) while Acura dropped by 2.5%. The year-to-date situation is a little better, as the premium brand has risen by 3.7% but only to a mere 114k units.
Anyway, it’s pretty clear that AHM wants to support Acura and make it more enticing for customers, with the premium brand now announcing “a new level of style, exclusivity and incredible value to its 2027 lineup,” all thanks to the introduction of the fresh but limited-edition Urban Spec trim for the Acura Integra, ADX, and MDX.
All versions mix the premium Urban Gray paint with exclusive gloss-black exterior details and larger wheels and tires for about $1,500 above the entry MSRP, “delivering standout design at an attractive price.” The new grade is reaching dealerships in December and will be presented to the public during the Los Angeles Auto Show (November 19-29), but official pricing details will arrive later, closer to the launch date.
"The new Acura Urban Spec trim is all about giving our customers standout design and added value across the Acura lineup," said Jessika Laudermilk, assistant vice president of Acura National Sales. "For Integra, ADX and MDX, we've brought together many of the design elements our customers love the most, creating limited-production Acura products that look special without a significant step up in price."
For the 2027 Acura Integra, the Urban Spec features include the Urban Gray paint, an Ebony interior, and Black 18-inch A-Spec wheels, wheel lugs, door handles, decklid spoiler, antenna, and badges. The 2027 ADX gets the Urban Gray paint, Ebony interior, optional AWD, and all the Black details except for the wheels, which grow to 19 inches.
Last but not least, the 2027 MDX packs the Urban Gray paint, Ebony interior, available SH-AWD, all the black details from the other two, plus the bumper and wheel well trim, along with even larger 20-inch A-Spec Advance wheels. So, what do you think?

United Kingdom Gets Volkswagen's First-Ever Full Hybrid Version of the Popular T-Roc Subcompact CUV
6 photos
Photo: Volkswagen AG
Better late than never applies to Volkswagen and its successful T-Roc subcompact crossover SUV: not long ago we wrote that the all-new, second-generation model is finally coming to Australia in early 2027 , almost two years after it was introduced to the world in the summer of 2025.
Now Volkswagen is finally joining the full hybrid game (!) in the United Kingdom with their first-ever full-hybrid model for the local market: the 2027 VW T-Roc Hybrid can be ordered from November 12 in the country. It also took them long enough: we signaled that the German automaker was finally moving into the regular hybrid powertrain space back in July 2026 when it announced the new powertrain on both the Golf and T-Roc.
Well, at least the United Kingdom is getting one of them – the Volkswagen T-Roc Hybrid will be available in three versions (Match, Style, and R-Line) with on-the-road recommended retail prices starting from £33,725 including VAT. That’s around $45k at the current exchange rate, which isn’t cheap by any standards – especially when the Chinese compete with the already established Western and Asian players for a piece of the pie and come with subversive pricing.
Anyway, Volkswagen offers the T-Roc Hybrid , which combines the ubiquitous 1.5 TSI engine with an electric battery and motor, sitting between the gasoline and PHEV models. “The T-Roc Hybrid is especially suitable for commuters in urban areas, where it combines enhanced fuel economy with low CO2 emissions and the smooth, comfortable driving experience of an electric vehicle,” says the brand, and it’s also compliant with the current ultra-low emission zone (ULEZ) requirements across the UK.
Customers will have a choice of three grades and two different powertrain versions: “the equipment-rich Match, sporty Style and the smart, polished R-Line.” Additionally, all feature the base HEV option of 136 combined ps (134 hp), while Style and R-Line also get a higher output of 170 ps (168 hp). The top version costs £40,500 ($54k), by the way.
All versions have a limited top speed of 112 mph (180 kph) and sprint to 62 mph or 100 kph in 9.7s for the base option or in 8.5s for the high-output variant. Standard features include 18-inch alloy wheels, rear privacy glass, automatic headlights, an eight-inch digital cockpit and 12.9-inch infotainment screen, AC, adaptive cruise control, automatic emergency braking with pedestrian and cyclist monitoring, and illuminated Volkswagen logos (Style and R-Line), among other things.
The second-generation Volkswagen T-Roc debuted in the UK earlier this year and has already collected various accolades, including Small SUV of the Year at the 2026 What Car? Awards, among other things. So, what do you think? Does the new Volkswagen T-Roc Hybrid stand a chance against the fierce competition across the United Kingdom or not?

source_document.body:
Photo: APMT Terminals Lazaro Cardenas
By Gavin van Marle
11 November 2026
Hapag-Lloyd has presented AMX, its new Asia–Mexico service, as standalone: its own ships; its own rotation of Ningbo-Qingdao-Busan-Ensenada-Manzanillo-Lázaro Cárdenas-Ningbo; launching in January 2027.
Standalone is the word the press release leans on, and it is the one worth questioning.
AMX is standalone the way a spoke is standalone – Hapag owns the vessels, but it can only fill an 8,000 teu ship on this run because the Gemini hub network it operates with Maersk gives the cargo somewhere to come from.
The question more important than what AMX actually is… is why Hapag can build it now and could not a few years ago.
Source: Hapag-Lloyd
Why Hapag couldn’t do this before
Owning the ships was never the hard part. Making a standalone loop work was, and that is what Gemini changed. Hapag has the Mexico cargo — its customers’ boxes already fill thousands of slots a week — but that cargo has been riding other lines’ ships, and a self-operated 8,000 teu loop has to be kept full in both directions and plugged into ports Hapag does not call directly.
The hub-and-spoke network it now runs with Maersk supplies the missing pieces – balancing cargo through the Gemini hubs and relay connections onward, so AMX does not have to source a full, self-sufficient ship at Asian load ports.
That option did not exist in a usable form until Gemini bedded in over the course of 2026. The simple answer to ‘why standalone’ and ‘why 2027’ is that the network to support a self-controlled spoke only recently came together.
This is not a one-off design. Hapag’s new Asia-South America east coast loop, ASX, is built the same way – a north Asian anchor port at Qingdao; no Shanghai call; and a relay through a Gemini hub.
AMX repeats that pattern to on the Pacific. Neither reads as a line striking out alone. Each is an owned loop made to clip onto the Gemini backbone, and the method is consistent — control the vessel, fill it through the hubs.
The next move is MSC’s
On the Mexico trade Hapag has not been sitting in a consortium at all. It has run its book by buying slots, chiefly from MSC, the largest carrier into the country.
That slice is not small: I estimate Hapag’s allocation on MSC’s loops is worth around 8,375 teu of nominal vessel capacity, call it some 7,000 teu of usable space for its customers once a ship is realistically loaded. Line that up against AMX, sized at 8,000 teu-9,000 teu, and the service looks less like new capacity than like Hapag rebuilding its existing slot block on its own hulls. The point of AMX may not primarily be to carry more, but to stop renting space from a direct rival.
That raises the question of what MSC next does? The slot deal is MSC’s to continue or end, and a carrier that has just watched its slot customer launch a competing service has every reason to reclaim the space and fill it with its own fast-growing Mexico cargo.
If MSC terminates, Hapag loses the slots it was already replacing with AMX and ends up roughly where it is today on capacity, albeit independent of a competitor’s deck. If MSC keeps selling, Hapag briefly holds both.
Either way the move is the same: a line that was depending on the market leader for space is buying its way out of that dependence.
Mexico’s pull is not new
Neither the demand levels nor this kind of service are new. CMA CGM ran the same play in May 2024, launching M2X, its Mexico Express, to almost exactly the ports Hapag has now chosen – in fact, AMX’s rotation differs from M2X’s original by a single North China port. The pull is still there.
Chinese manufacturers have kept building in Mexico to serve the United States from inside the USMCA wall and to sell into Mexico itself, though the frantic investment of 2023–24 has since cooled, probably unsurprisingly.
Which means Hapag is – two and a half years later – responding to the signal CMA answered first with a near-identical loop, into ports that are already stretched.
The cautionary note sits in the same data: CMA CGM has lost more Mexican import share than any carrier over these years, even while running its own loop.
A ship of one’s own controls the cargo without guaranteeing you keep it.

To grow into a biopharma juggernaut, China aims to become the leading source of innovative medicines on the global markets—a goal that experts say the country is on track to hit.
China’s latest five-year plan to grow its domestic biopharma sector includes a set of goals that are largely within reach, experts told BioSpace —especially the country’s ambition to become a leading innovative engine for global biopharma, not merely a provider of cheap copycat drugs.
“I have no doubt China will meet its goal,” Claudia Lin, founder of Biotech East West Technical Services, told BioSpace in an email.
That said, some of the targets laid out in the country’s most recent five-year plan, released by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology in September, will be easier to attain than others.
Lin believes, for instance, that the Asian giant is all but guaranteed to have five blockbusters by the end of the decade and is on track to clear its 2030 revenue target of 3.5 trillion yuan ($521.8 billion). On the other hand, having 50 domestic drugmakers with 10 billion yuan ($1.5 billion) in annual revenue could be a tough target, said Cody Powers, principal at the management consulting firm ZS.
Most of China’s heaviest hitters have been generating sales within the country, he explained, but “reaching this new milestone likely means many more companies expanding abroad.”

China plans to transform biotech sector into $522B powerhouse by 2030
A new five-year biotech plan has been released by the Chinese government, revealing ambitious goals such as achieving five blockbuster medicines on the global markets in that time.
September 18, 2026
·
2 min read
·
Annalee Armstrong
Read more
A long time coming
China’s rise as a go-to destination for biotech innovation and early-stage development has been strategic. The Asian country has long been releasing five-year plans for its biotech industry—the first came out in 2007—plotting priorities and specific goals to promote and guide the growth of its domestic drug development sector.
China has been “executing superbly” on its biopharma roadmap, Jeremy Levin, co-founder and executive chair of Ovid Therapeutics, said during a BioSpace webinar on China last month. “They’re faster, they’re better, they are doing what they said they’d do.”
China’s share of global licensing deal value this year has shot up to 58% , from 14% in 2023, according to an October report from global investment bank Locust Walk, as biopharma earmarks billions of dollars in partnerships with Chinese companies. “Any concept that they can’t do innovation is nonsense,” Levin said.
This despite increasing geopolitical pressures, including actions in the U.S. like the BIOSECURE Act that seek to restrict American companies from working with “foreign adversary biotech companies,” such as those in China.
China
China’s surging biotech sector represents both competition and lifeline for the US
As Chinese companies push beyond “me-too” drugs and the country lays out a new five-year plan targeting a $522 billion–strong biotech industry by 2030, experts say more predictable funding and regulation could help the U.S. maintain its edge.
September 23, 2026
·
8 min read
·
Shawna Williams
Read more
More recently, the U.S. Department of Treasury has proposed limiting outbound investments to biotech entities in certain countries of concern—a list that includes China. This measure, however, carves out a key exemption for licensing deals.
Such policy initiatives are therefore unlikely to stall China’s continued growth—or stop it from hitting its next set of goals, the foundation for which has already been laid.
“China has set itself a target that most likely it would achieve without any further action on its part,” Mark Lansdell, director at life sciences analytics firm Evaluate, told BioSpace in an email. “The achievement of China’s end-of-decade goal was determined by actions that took place in the first years of the decade.”
China
China’s licensing deals soar as US biotechs enjoy a bumper M&A year
China may be taking the majority of licensing deals this year but those transactions don’t tell the whole story, according to Locust Walk, which points to the spike in M&A among U.S. biotechs as leveling the playing field.
October 21, 2026
·
3 min read
·
Annalee Armstrong
Read more
Not without challenges, need for changes
That said, the road will by no means be frictionless—and some of the country’s goals will prove more challenging than others. Achieving 50 homegrown companies with $1.5 billion in revenue will be “the hardest to hit,” according to ZS’ Powers.
“There’s already a decent-sized list of companies at that level,” Powers told BioSpace over email. This includes Hengrui Pharmaceuticals ($4.74 billion revenue in 2025), Fosun Pharma ($6.25 billion) and Hansoh Pharmaceutical ($2.25 billion).
To cross the 50 mark, China will likely need to change its approach to dealmaking, Powers said. Currently, the country’s dominant model has been to license out worldwide rights to domestically developed drugs, collecting only local revenue once drugs hit the market. To top $1.5 billion, Powers argued, Chinese biotechs will need to retain ex-China ownership of the drugs they make. “If companies just out-license, it will be pretty hard to reach that goal.”
Aside from a shift in partnership strategy, there are also some broader, cultural changes that need to happen for China to truly grow into a global biopharma powerhouse, Biotech East West Technical Services’ Lin said. “China has always won world-class status by its speed, cost and volume,” she said. Now, the country “needs to shift the culture surrounding the industry and [make] quality a focus.”
Lin recognizes that China has made major improvements in quality and compliance over the years, particularly after joining the International Council for Harmonization—a global group that sets quality standards for producing pharmaceuticals—in 2017.
Still, novel therapeutic modalities are proving challenging for the country’s ascendant biotech sector, Lin said, pointing to the need to ensure that these cutting-edge technologies are safe and effective, and that data generated from their studies are reliable.
Of course, a more aggressive push to expand ownership overseas is likely to be met by pushback from other countries, Powers recognizes. Meeting this 50-company goal, therefore, also depends on “whether U.S. and European policymakers restrict that growth through trade policy,” he said. “[Future] policy obstacles as the trade war expands into biopharma could hinder launches or otherwise act as a headwind.”
And given that vulnerability, China would do well to “improve domestic economics,” in addition to expanding into overseas markets, Powers argued. He noted that the country’s healthcare authorities have continued to negotiate lower prices, cutting into biopharma companies’ domestic revenue.
Five blockbusters only ‘a matter of time’
Of all of China’s 2030 goals, having five blockbusters appears most achievable. Meeting the target “is largely now a matter of time,” Evaluate’s Lansdell said.
For a drug to have a good chance of making $1 billion by 2030, it needs to already be on the market or in late-stage development, which means China laid the groundwork for this goal years ago. “The wheels have already been set in motion,” Lansdell explained.
Evaluate’s internal data projects at least six blockbusters for China by the end of the decade—two of which have already crossed that bar and just need to maintain their market performance. These include BeOne Medicines’ BTK inhibitor Brukinsa, which made $3.9 billion last year , and Legend Biotech’s Johnson & Johnson-partnered CAR T therapy Carvykti, with $1.9 billion in 2025 sales .
Behind these, the products likely to cross the blockbuster line by 2030 are BeOne Medicines’ PD-1 inhibitor Tevimbra —approved in the U.S. for esophageal and gastric cancers and forecast to pass $1 billion in annual sales as early as next year—and Summit Therapeutics’ Akeso-partnered ivonescimab, a PD-1xVEGF bispecific antibody that Evaluate estimates will hit $4.4 billion in sales between the partners by 2030.

EICMA 2026 • Triumph TF-E Bikes Get Even More Enduro With Updates for the 2027 Model Year
Citroen Augments Its New C5 and e-C5 Aircross SUV Ranges With Fresh Emerald Trim Level in the UK
6 photos
Photo: Citroen
Order books have already opened for the new flagship trim level for the United Kingdom market for the Citroen New C5 and e-C5 Aircross crossover SUVs, with pricing starting from £37,290 MRRP, which is about $50k at the current exchange rate. Ouch, right?
If you have been wondering what Citroen has been up to across the UK market as of late, the answer is simple: not much. Instead, they have simply relied on the global news: Sandeep Bhambra’s appointment as Head of Design for Citroen and DS Automobiles, the 2CV Concept along with the sibling Furgonnette prototype striking a chord with the audience at the 2026 Paris Motor Show, or the company’s introduction of the fresh Outdoor trim level for the C3, e-C3, C3 Aircross and its fully electric version.
Well, now it’s time for a change, and Citroen UK has announced the expansion of the New C5 Aircross lineup with the introduction of the Emerald grade, now the flagship trim level for the hybrid and electric variants. Emerald trim becomes the highest specification option for both, exceeding the previous Max configuration that it builds upon with Drive Assist Pack 2.0, Head-Up Display, and heated front seats and steering wheel, among others.
The new trim also marks the introduction of a new premium Emerald Blue metallic paint option, priced at £645 incl. VAT. The Emerald version adds a black roof and Emerald-coloured clips on the front bumper and doors. In the cabin there’s a panoramic opening sunroof, a frameless electrochrome rear-view mirror, grey leather-effect and cloth Advanced Comfort seats, plus Emerald interior detailing and lighting.
The company also offers a suspension with Progressive Hydraulic Cushions, as well as a wide array of powertrain options. For example, the Citroen e-C5 Aircross Emerald comes with the 210hp Comfort Range and up to 321 miles (WLTP combined) of range, starting from £38,845 ($52k) with the Electric Car Grant, while the 230hp Long Range version offers up to 421 miles (WLTP combined) of range from £44,965 or $60k.
Citroen says it maintains a level of affordability, but who are they kidding? These are premium prices; there’s no doubt about it. At least the C5 Aircross Emerald also comes with a meager Hybrid 145 powertrain from £37,290 or a plug-in hybrid version with 195 ponies from £39,860 or $53k. Additionally, the Hybrid Plus, Max, and Emerald variants have a new 19-inch moondust diamond-cut silver and black alloy wheel model.
“We are excited about the addition of the Emerald trim level, both for its vibrant new shade which perfectly complements the lines of the C5 Aircross, and for its generous level of equipment, including a panoramic sunroof. This trim level marks a continued development of our product range, bringing a more premium specification at an affordable price point,” said Greg Taylor, Managing Director, Citroen UK.
